community.title: Christ — The Centre of All Scripture
community.emph: Understand that the entire Bible points to Jesus Christ and God's plan of salvation.

lessons.t: God's Redemption Plan from Genesis to Revelation
lessons.hint: Show the Bible as one unfolding story of God's redemption, with Christ as its centre rather than treating the Bible as disconnected moral stories.
obj: Trace the promise of redemption from Genesis to Revelation.
See how prophecy, promise, sacrifice and fulfilment point toward Christ.
Understand that the cross is not an isolated event but the centre of God's redemptive plan.
out: The fall and the need for redemption.
The promise of the woman's offspring.
The prophetic picture of the suffering Servant.
Christ's death and resurrection as fulfilment.
Revelation's picture of the Lamb who was slain.
app: Read the Old Testament with Christ in view.
Avoid teaching Bible characters merely as examples of success; ask what the passage reveals about God, sin, redemption and Christ.
Help learners connect the whole counsel of Scripture.

faq.q: Why is Christ central to the whole Bible?
faq.a: Because Scripture presents God's unfolding redemptive purpose, which reaches its fulfilment in Christ. Jesus Himself explained the Scriptures in relation to His suffering and glory (Luke 24:26–27).

faq.q: Does every Old Testament verse directly mention Jesus?
faq.a: No. A sound approach respects the original context while recognising the larger redemptive storyline that Scripture itself connects to Christ.

lessons.t: Christ Revealed in the Old Testament
lessons.hint: Use biblical types and patterns carefully: the Passover Lamb, the bronze serpent and Melchizedek help illuminate Christ without ignoring their original historical meaning.
obj: Recognise major Old Testament pictures fulfilled or clarified in Christ.
Learn to connect Old Testament passages to New Testament explanations.
Distinguish biblical typology from imaginative symbolism.
out: The bronze serpent and Jesus' explanation.
Melchizedek and the priesthood of Christ.
How the New Testament interprets Old Testament patterns.
app: When teaching a type, first explain the Old Testament passage in context.
Then show the New Testament connection.
Keep Christ at the centre without forcing symbolism into every detail.

faq.q: Why is the Passover important for understanding Christ?
faq.a: The New Testament identifies Christ with sacrificial Passover imagery, highlighting deliverance through His sacrifice (1 Corinthians 5:7).

faq.q: Why did Jesus refer to the bronze serpent?
faq.a: In John 3:14–15, Jesus used Moses' lifted serpent to explain that the Son of Man would be lifted up so that believers may have life.

lessons.hint: Teach Jesus not simply as a teacher or miracle worker, but as the Word who became flesh, revealing the Father and accomplishing the Father's mission.
obj: Examine His teachings and miracles as signs of the Kingdom.
app: When teaching the Gospels, ask what the passage reveals about who Jesus is.
Connect His works to His mission rather than treating miracles as entertainment.
Invite learners to respond to Christ, not merely admire Him.

faq.q: What is the main purpose of the Gospel accounts?
faq.a: They bear witness to Jesus and call people to faith in Him; John explicitly states this purpose in John 20:30–31.

faq.q: Why are Jesus' miracles important?
faq.a: They reveal His authority and identity and point people toward the Kingdom and faith in Him.

lessons.hint: Keep Christ as the Head of the Church: the Church does not replace Christ, but belongs to Him, receives life from Him and represents Him in the world.
obj: Recognise the Church's calling to reflect Christ.
app: Evaluate church life by faithfulness to Christ and His Word.
Teach service as a response to belonging to Christ.
Avoid making personalities, programmes or institutions the centre.

faq.q: What does it mean that Christ is Head of the Church?
faq.a: Christ has supreme authority over His Church; the Church receives its direction and identity from Him.

faq.q: How do believers live in union with Christ?
faq.a: By abiding in Him through faith, obedience and dependence, like branches remain connected to the vine (John 15:1–5).

community.title: The Finished Work of Christ
community.emph: Explain Christ's completed work on the Cross and its significance for salvation and Christian living.

lessons.hint: Explain the seriousness of sin, God's righteousness and the sacrificial work of Christ without reducing the cross to a vague example of love.
obj: Understand the necessity and meaning of Christ's death.
See the cross as God's provision for reconciliation.
out: God's righteousness and mercy meet at the cross.
app: Teach both God's holiness and God's mercy.
Keep the cross central when explaining salvation.
Do not present salvation as something earned by human merit.

faq.q: Did Jesus die because God was unable to forgive without sacrifice?
faq.a: Scripture presents the cross as God's own gracious provision through which He remains righteous while justifying those who have faith in Jesus (Romans 3:25–26).

faq.q: What does Christ's death accomplish?
faq.a: It addresses sin and opens the way for forgiveness, reconciliation and justification through faith.

lessons.hint: Show that Jesus' declaration points to the completion of His assigned work, not to defeat or resignation.
obj: Understand the significance of Christ's final declaration.
out: The work Christ came to accomplish.
The believer's response to a finished work.
app: Teach believers to rest in Christ's completed work while continuing in obedient discipleship.
Distinguish salvation accomplished by Christ from spiritual growth lived out by the believer.

faq.q: Does 'finished' mean Christians no longer need to obey God?
faq.a: No. The finished work establishes salvation; believers then live in grateful obedience and holiness.

faq.q: What should the believer do with a finished work?
faq.a: Trust Christ, receive His grace, reject self-righteousness and live from the new life He gives.

lessons.t: The Benefits of Christ's Finished Work
lessons.hint: Help learners understand justification, reconciliation and adoption as concrete results of God's saving work in Christ.
app: Teach the benefits as realities grounded in Christ, not as promises detached from Him.
Help learners distinguish justification from the process of sanctification.

faq.q: What is justification?
faq.a: It is God's gracious declaration of righteousness for the believer through faith in Christ.

faq.q: What is reconciliation?
faq.a: It describes restored relationship with God through Christ, who brings peace between God and those who trust Him.

lessons.t: Living in the Victory of Christ
lessons.hint: Move from doctrine to daily life: believers live from Christ's victory, freedom from condemnation and new life by the Spirit.
app: Do not use grace as permission for sin.
Do not use failure as proof that Christ has abandoned the believer.
Point repeatedly to Christ's work and the Spirit's transforming work.

faq.q: Does freedom from condemnation mean sin no longer matters?
faq.a: No. Sin still matters, but believers are no longer under condemnation in Christ and are called to walk in the Spirit.

faq.q: What does 'Christ lives in me' mean practically?
faq.a: It means the believer's life is now lived in dependence on Christ, shaped by faith, love and obedience.

community.title: The Believer's Identity in Christ
community.emph: Discover who believers are through Christ and live confidently in that identity.

lessons.t: Knowing Who You Are in Christ
lessons.hint: Teach identity as something received from God in Christ, not constructed from past failures, achievements, social labels or other people's opinions.
obj: Understand what it means to be in Christ.
Recognise the old self/new creation contrast.
Learn to live from identity rather than earn identity.
out: The old self versus the new creation.
app: Reject labels that contradict God's Word.
Practise speaking and living in agreement with Scripture.
Use identity in Christ as a foundation for confidence and humility.

faq.q: Does being a new creation mean my past never happened?
faq.a: No. It means the past no longer defines the believer's standing before God; Christ gives a new identity and direction.

faq.q: How should identity in Christ affect daily life?
faq.a: It should shape choices, relationships, confidence, holiness and service.

lessons.hint: Teach adoption as a privilege and relationship: believers belong to God's family and are called to live accordingly.
obj: Recognise responsibilities of belonging to God's family.
app: Approach God with confidence and reverence.
Treat fellow believers as family.
Teach inheritance together with responsibility.

faq.q: Can believers really call God Father?
faq.a: Yes. Scripture describes believers as adopted children and teaches them to approach God as Father.

faq.q: What responsibility comes with being God's child?
faq.a: Believers are called to reflect the Father's character, love fellow believers and walk in obedience.

lessons.t: The Temple of the Holy Spirit
lessons.hint: Teach the indwelling Holy Spirit as a call to holiness, wise stewardship of the body and sensitivity to God's guidance.
obj: Appreciate the Spirit's guidance and fruit.
out: Caring for body, mind and soul.
app: Make choices that honour God.
Cultivate sensitivity to the Spirit through Scripture and prayer.
Look for the fruit of the Spirit rather than merely dramatic experiences.

faq.q: What does it mean that the body is a temple?
faq.a: The believer belongs to God and should honour Him with the body and the whole of life.

faq.q: How do we become sensitive to the Spirit?
faq.a: By remaining attentive to God's Word, prayer, obedience and the Spirit's fruit and conviction.

lessons.hint: Show that identity produces mission: those reconciled to God are entrusted with representing Christ and the ministry of reconciliation.
out: Representing Christ in words and actions.
app: Share the Gospel courageously.
Reflect Christ's love in family, work and community.
Let character support the message.

faq.q: What makes a Christian an ambassador?
faq.a: God entrusts reconciled believers with the message and ministry of reconciliation.

faq.q: Must every believer preach publicly?
faq.a: Every believer is called to witness to Christ, although forms of service and ministry differ among believers.

community.title: Walking in Faith and Obedience to God's Word
community.emph: Understand the relationship between faith, obedience and discipleship.

lessons.hint: Define faith as trust in God that rests on His character and promises and expresses itself in faithful living.
obj: See faith as response to God.
out: Faith comes through hearing God's Word.
app: Teach faith from God's revelation, not from human certainty about desired outcomes.
Encourage trust even when circumstances are unresolved.

faq.q: Is faith simply believing hard enough?
faq.a: Biblical faith is trust in God; it is not merely mental intensity or positive thinking.

faq.q: What strengthens faith?
faq.a: Hearing and receiving God's Word and remembering His faithfulness strengthens faith.

lessons.hint: Show that genuine faith produces action; obedience is evidence of living faith, not a substitute for grace.
app: Ask what obedience follows from every teaching session.
Avoid teaching works as a means of purchasing salvation.

faq.q: Do works save us?
faq.a: Scripture teaches salvation by grace through faith, while also teaching that genuine faith is living and produces works.

faq.q: Why does Jesus connect love and obedience?
faq.a: John 14:15 presents obedience as a response of love to Christ.

lessons.hint: Identify fear, doubt, disappointment, distraction and spiritual opposition as pressures that can test faith, while directing attention back to Christ.
obj: Learn biblical responses to fear and doubt.
app: Create space for honest questions without celebrating unbelief.
Use Scripture to re-anchor the heart in Christ.

faq.q: Does doubt automatically mean there is no faith?
faq.a: Scripture records faithful people bringing questions and fears to God. Faith learns to bring doubt into God's presence rather than hide it.

faq.q: What should we do when afraid?
faq.a: Bring fear to God, remember His character and continue trusting and obeying Him.

lessons.hint: Turn faith from a Sunday idea into a daily posture of trust, prayer, obedience and dependence.
app: Encourage practical acts of obedience.
Teach learners to seek God's wisdom rather than merely ask God to endorse their plans.

faq.q: How do I live by faith in ordinary decisions?
faq.a: Bring decisions to God, search Scripture for principles, seek wise counsel and act obediently.

faq.q: Does faith remove uncertainty?
faq.a: Not always. Faith means trusting God even when the full outcome is not known.

community.title: Understanding God's Grace and Mercy
community.emph: Differentiate grace and mercy and appreciate their role in redemption and daily living.

lessons.hint: Explain grace as God's undeserved favour and saving initiative, while showing that grace produces a transformed life.
obj: See grace as a teacher of holy living.
app: Reject both self-righteousness and cheap grace.
Let gratitude for grace produce obedience.

faq.q: Does grace mean God ignores sin?
faq.a: No. Grace addresses sin through God's saving work and trains believers to reject ungodliness.

faq.q: Can good works earn grace?
faq.a: No. Grace is undeserved; good works are a response to God's saving grace.

lessons.hint: Help learners recognise God's compassion toward those in need and His repeated mercies.
app: Cultivate gratitude for God's mercy.
Respond to others with compassion rather than harshness.

faq.q: Is mercy the same as grace?
faq.a: They overlap but are not identical: grace emphasises undeserved favour, while mercy emphasises compassion and withholding deserved judgment.

faq.q: Why can believers approach God's throne boldly?
faq.a: Hebrews 4:16 invites believers to approach because of Christ's priestly ministry and God's mercy and grace.

lessons.hint: Teach grace as an active teacher that shapes conduct, not merely a doctrine about forgiveness.
app: Ask: 'How should God's grace change this decision?'
Give God credit for spiritual progress.

faq.q: Can someone use grace as an excuse to continue sinning?
faq.a: Paul rejects that idea in Romans 6:1–2.

faq.q: How should grace affect ministry?
faq.a: It should produce humility, generosity and dependence on God rather than boasting.

lessons.hint: Move from receiving mercy to becoming instruments of mercy in relationships, conflict and restoration.
app: Be compassionate without abandoning truth or healthy boundaries.
Pray for grace to respond rather than retaliate.

faq.q: Does mercy mean there should never be consequences?
faq.a: No. Mercy and justice are not identical; mercy can coexist with appropriate accountability.

faq.q: Why should Christians show mercy?
faq.a: Because they themselves live by God's mercy and are called to reflect His character.

community.title: Growing in Spiritual Maturity
community.emph: Learn the importance of continual spiritual growth and maturity in Christ.

lessons.hint: Make spiritual growth a continuing Christian responsibility: knowing Christ more deeply and becoming more like Him.
app: Measure growth by increasing Christlikeness, obedience, love and discernment, not only by activity or information.

faq.q: Can a Christian stop growing?
faq.a: A believer can become stagnant, but Scripture calls Christians to continual growth.

faq.q: What is spiritual maturity?
faq.a: It includes increasing knowledge of Christ, stable faith, discernment, obedience and Christlike character.

lessons.hint: Teach prayer, Scripture, fasting and worship as means of cultivating relationship with God—not as ways to earn His acceptance.
obj: Understand the purpose of spiritual disciplines.
app: Keep the disciplines Christ-centred.
Avoid legalism and comparison.
Encourage realistic, sustainable habits.

faq.q: Are spiritual disciplines a way to earn salvation?
faq.a: No. They are practices that help believers seek God and grow; salvation is God's grace.

faq.q: Which discipline should come first?
faq.a: There is no single formula, but prayer and Scripture provide foundational ways of knowing and responding to God.

lessons.t: Bearing the Fruit of the Spirit
lessons.hint: Focus on transformed character rather than merely outward religious activity.
obj: Identify the fruit of the Spirit.
Understand the conflict between flesh and Spirit.
app: Choose one fruit to practise intentionally.
Use relationships as opportunities for spiritual growth.
Connect fruit to the Spirit's work, not self-effort alone.

faq.q: Is the fruit of the Spirit nine separate fruits?
faq.a: Galatians presents them together as the fruit produced by the Spirit.

faq.q: How does fruit grow?
faq.a: Jesus connects fruitfulness with abiding in Him; the Spirit produces Christlike character as believers walk with Him.

lessons.hint: Teach maturity as endurance, discernment and faithful progress even when growth is difficult.
app: Encourage learners not to abandon growth during difficult seasons.
Create opportunities to practise discernment and obedience.

faq.q: Does hardship mean a believer is failing spiritually?
faq.a: Not necessarily. Scripture teaches that trials can produce endurance and maturity.

faq.q: How can discernment grow?
faq.a: Through consistent engagement with God's Word and practice in distinguishing good from evil.

community.title: The Holy Spirit and His Work in the Believer
community.emph: Know the Holy Spirit as a divine Person, and understand what he does in the believer and in the Church.

lessons.hint: Teach the Holy Spirit as a divine Person to be known and obeyed, not as a force, an atmosphere or a feeling that comes and goes with the music.
obj: Know the Holy Spirit as the third Person of the Blessed Trinity.
Distinguish the Person of the Spirit from his effects and manifestations.
Understand that he dwells in the believer and remains.
out: The Spirit is a Person: he teaches, speaks, grieves, wills and sends.
The Spirit in the life of Jesus, from the Jordan to the Cross.
The Spirit given to the Church at Pentecost and in Baptism and Confirmation.
app: Speak of the Spirit as 'he', never as 'it'.
Do not judge his presence by atmosphere or emotion.
Teach believers to ask, listen and obey, which is how a Person is related to.

faq.q: Is the Holy Spirit a power or a Person?
faq.a: A divine Person. Scripture says he teaches, bears witness, intercedes, forbids, sends and can be grieved — all the acts of a person, not of a force.

faq.q: Does the Holy Spirit leave a believer who sins?
faq.a: The Spirit dwells in the baptised believer and is grieved by sin rather than driven away by every fall; serious sin wounds the relationship, and repentance restores it.

ccc.q: it is Christ who is seen, the visible image of the invisible God, but it is the Spirit who reveals him

lessons.hint: Show that the Spirit's work always leads to Christ. Any spirituality that moves attention away from Christ is not the work of the Holy Spirit, however impressive it looks.
obj: Understand the Spirit's work of glorifying Christ.
Learn to test spiritual claims by whether they exalt Christ and agree with Scripture.
See the Spirit as the one who makes the Scriptures living to us.
out: He will guide you into all truth.
He shall glorify me: the Spirit's chosen work.
The Spirit and the written Word together.
Testing the spirits: the rule of 1 John 4.
app: Test every teaching and manifestation by Christ and the Scriptures.
Pray for the Spirit's light before study, not only before preaching.
Refuse any teaching that makes an experience greater than Christ.

faq.q: How do I know whether something is from the Holy Spirit?
faq.a: Ask what it does with Christ and with Scripture. The Spirit glorifies Christ and never contradicts the word he inspired.

faq.q: Does the Spirit still speak today?
faq.a: Yes, but never with a new gospel. Whatever he says agrees with what he has already said in Scripture and in the faith handed down.

ccc.q: Christianity is the religion of the "Word" of God
ccc.note: not a religion of the book, but of the living Word

lessons.t: The Fruit of the Spirit and Christian Character
lessons.hint: Keep character above display. Fruit is the evidence the New Testament asks us to look for, and it grows slowly in ordinary life.
obj: Name and understand the fruit of the Spirit.
Distinguish fruit from gift and from temperament.
See how fruit is formed through daily walking in the Spirit.
out: The works of the flesh and the fruit of the Spirit.
Fruit is singular: one life, many flavours.
Walking in the Spirit as a daily practice.
app: Judge spiritual growth by love, patience and self-control, not by platform.
Give new believers time; fruit ripens.
Correct the teacher whose gift outruns his character.

faq.q: Can someone have great gifts and poor character?
faq.a: Yes, and Scripture warns about it. Gifts are given; fruit is grown. The Lord tells us we shall know them by their fruits.

faq.q: Why am I not growing faster?
faq.a: Fruit ripens in ordinary circumstances, often the difficult ones. Keep abiding: the branch's work is to stay joined to the vine.

lessons.t: Gifts for the Building Up of the Church
lessons.hint: Teach the gifts as given for others, measured by love and order, and belonging to the whole body rather than to a spiritual class.
obj: Understand the variety and purpose of spiritual gifts.
Learn the rule of love and the rule of order.
Recognise that every believer is given something for the common good.
out: Diversities of gifts, the same Spirit.
To every man for the profit of all.
Love as the more excellent way.
app: Never grade believers by which gift they have.
Measure every exercise of a gift by whether the Church was built up.
Keep gatherings orderly so that visitors are helped and not confused.

faq.q: Are the gifts still given today?
faq.a: Yes. The Church has never taught that the Spirit stopped giving, and our renewal exists largely because believers took that seriously.

faq.q: Is a person without a visible gift less spiritual?
faq.a: No. The manifestation of the Spirit is given to every man to profit withal, and love is the measure, not visibility.

community.title: Living a Christ-Centred Christian Life
community.emph: Bring the whole of life — home, work, prayer and witness — under the lordship of Christ.

lessons.t: Christ at the Centre of Daily Life
lessons.hint: Move the lesson from Sunday to Monday. A Christ-centred life is not a more religious life; it is the ordinary day lived in union with Christ.
obj: Understand what it means to seek the things above.
See the believer's life as hidden with Christ in God.
Identify the places where Christ is not yet at the centre.
out: Risen with Christ: the ground of daily living.
Setting the mind, and why the mind decides the day.
Your life is hid with Christ in God.
app: Begin the day by deliberately setting the mind on Christ.
Name one area — money, speech, temper, time — and bring it under his lordship this week.
Resist the split between 'church life' and 'real life'.

faq.q: Does a Christ-centred life mean leaving secular work?
faq.a: No. It means doing that work as unto the Lord. Most Christians are sanctified exactly where they already are.

faq.q: Is it wrong to enjoy ordinary things?
faq.a: No. Christ at the centre orders our loves; it does not abolish them. Every good thing is received with thanksgiving.

lessons.t: Christ in the Home and at Work
lessons.hint: Teach that the household and the workplace are the ordinary places of holiness, and resist the idea that only ministry counts as service to God.
obj: Apply the lordship of Christ to family relationships.
Understand work as service rendered to the Lord.
Recognise honesty and diligence as Christian witness.
out: Whatsoever ye do, in word or deed.
The Christian household: honour, patience, forgiveness.
Work done heartily, as to the Lord.
Integrity in a place where it costs something.
app: Let the family see the same person they hear praying.
Refuse dishonest practice even where everyone accepts it.
Treat those who work for you as the Lord treats you.

faq.q: Is my secular job a lesser calling?
faq.a: No. Scripture addresses ordinary workers directly and tells them their work is service to Christ.

faq.q: What if honesty costs me the job or the contract?
faq.a: Then it costs. Scripture never promises that integrity is cheap, and it never permits us to buy comfort with dishonesty.

lessons.t: Prayer, the Sacraments and the Word
lessons.hint: Show the ordinary means by which the Christian life is sustained, and keep them joined: the word read, the Eucharist received, prayer made, fellowship kept.
obj: Understand the pattern of the first believers.
See prayer, word and sacrament as one life, not competing options.
Build a simple, sustainable rule of life.
out: They continued steadfastly: the four marks of Acts 2:42.
The breaking of bread and the life of grace.
app: Help each member set a simple daily rule they can actually keep.
Join Scripture to the Sunday readings so the week and the liturgy agree.
Keep fellowship: nobody grows alone.

faq.q: Is Bible study enough on its own?
faq.a: No. The first believers gave themselves to teaching, fellowship, the breaking of bread and prayer together. Remove one and the life weakens.

faq.q: How much should I pray and read?
faq.a: Begin with what you will actually do every day. A small rule kept faithfully builds more than a large one abandoned in a week.

lessons.t: Witness: Christ Seen in the Believer
lessons.hint: End the series by sending people out. Witness is not a department of the Church; it is what a Christ-centred life does naturally.
obj: Understand the believer as light and as a letter of Christ.
Learn to give an account of our hope simply and respectfully.
See witness as life and word together.
out: Ye are the light of the world.
Known and read of all men.
Giving a reason for the hope that is in you.
Where our witness is most needed: family, street, office, parish.
app: Name one person to pray for and speak to this month.
Let the manner of the witness match the message: with meekness and fear.
Let the parish see a people whose lives agree with their teaching.

faq.q: What if I am not a preacher?
faq.a: Witness is not preaching. It is a life people can read, and a simple account of your hope when you are asked.

faq.q: Must I argue people into faith?
faq.a: No. Peter says to give a reason with meekness and reverence. Arguments win points; a reasoned, gentle answer wins people.

reserve.title: The Hope of Glory
reserve.emph: Understand Christ dwelling in believers and the hope of eternal glory.

lessons.hint: Teach the believer's hope as Christ's presence and promise, not merely optimism about circumstances.
obj: Connect present life with future hope.
app: When circumstances are discouraging, anchor hope in Christ rather than changing conditions.

faq.q: What is the hope of glory?
faq.a: It is the confident hope connected with Christ and the promised glory He brings.

faq.q: How should this hope affect today?
faq.a: It should produce perseverance, holiness and confidence in Christ.

lessons.hint: Teach eternal life as God's promise in Christ and encourage believers to live in expectation of Christ's return.
obj: Understand the biblical promise of eternal life.
app: Avoid speculation about dates and details.
Keep attention on Christ and faithful living.

faq.q: What gives believers hope of eternal life?
faq.a: God's promise in Christ and the testimony of Scripture.

faq.q: Does future hope make present life less important?
faq.a: No. It motivates faithful living and good works while believers await Christ.

lessons.hint: Teach believers to interpret present suffering and success in light of eternity.
app: Use eternity to correct unhealthy attachment to status, possessions and temporary success.

faq.q: Does eternal perspective mean ignoring present responsibilities?
faq.a: No. It means fulfilling present responsibilities while valuing what lasts eternally.

faq.q: How does eternal hope help in suffering?
faq.a: It does not deny pain; it places suffering within the larger hope of God's promised glory.

lessons.t: Encouraging Others with the Hope of Glory
lessons.hint: Equip believers to use Christian hope to strengthen people facing grief, uncertainty and discouragement.
app: Do not offer shallow explanations of suffering.
Use Scripture to comfort and point to Christ and God's promises.

faq.q: How can we comfort someone grieving?
faq.a: Be present, listen, pray and use the hope of Christ and resurrection with sensitivity.

faq.q: Why is Christian hope powerful?
faq.a: It rests on God's promises and Christ's victory, giving believers reason to persevere.

reserve.title: When God Is Silent
reserve.emph: Learn how to trust God during seasons of delay and unanswered prayers.

lessons.hint: Help believers distinguish God's apparent silence from God's absence and learn to bring honest lament to Him.
obj: Keep relationship with God during delay.
app: Give permission for honest prayer while maintaining trust.
Do not claim to know God's hidden reasons without biblical support.

faq.q: Does silence mean God has rejected me?
faq.a: Not necessarily. Scripture contains seasons where faithful people experienced God's apparent silence while continuing to trust Him.

faq.q: Can I tell God that I am hurting?
faq.a: Yes. The Psalms model honest lament directed toward God.

lessons.hint: Show persistent faith through the Canaanite woman's encounter with Jesus, while handling the passage carefully and respectfully.
app: Teach persistence without promising a specific outcome.
Keep Christ's character and God's wisdom central.

faq.q: Why continue praying if there is no answer?
faq.a: Because prayer is relationship with God, and Scripture repeatedly calls believers to persevere.

faq.q: Does persistence force God's hand?
faq.a: No. Persistent prayer expresses trust and dependence; God remains sovereign.

lessons.hint: Teach waiting as active trust rather than passive frustration, without using 'God's timing' to dismiss genuine pain.
app: Help learners identify what obedience looks like while waiting.
Avoid making unsupported promises about when a specific answer will come.

faq.q: Why does God sometimes delay?
faq.a: Scripture gives different reasons in different contexts; believers should avoid pretending to know God's hidden purposes in every case.

faq.q: What should I do while waiting?
faq.a: Continue praying, obeying, serving and trusting God.

lessons.hint: Prepare believers to receive God's answers with humility—whether the answer is yes, no, wait or something different from what was expected.
obj: Understand that prayer is submission to God.
app: Do not teach formulas that guarantee outcomes.
Encourage submission to God's wisdom and continued relationship with Him.

faq.q: What if God says no?
faq.a: A 'no' does not mean God is uncaring; Scripture shows Paul receiving grace in an answer different from his request.

faq.q: How do I remain faithful after disappointment?
faq.a: Bring the disappointment honestly to God and continue trusting His character and promises.

reserve.title: The Character of Peter
reserve.emph: Study Peter's transformation from impulsive disciple to courageous apostle.

lessons.hint: Show how Jesus called an ordinary, imperfect person and gradually shaped him into a witness and leader.
app: Avoid turning Peter into a flawless hero; keep Jesus as the One who calls and transforms.

faq.q: Why did Jesus choose Peter?
faq.a: The passage emphasises Jesus' initiative in calling him; Peter's later growth demonstrates God's transforming work.

faq.q: Was Peter immediately mature?
faq.a: No. His life shows growth, mistakes, correction, restoration and service.

lessons.hint: Teach failure honestly while showing Christ's restoring grace and renewed commission.
obj: Learn from failure without remaining trapped by it.
app: Do not shame people with their failures.
Do not minimise failure either; show repentance, restoration and renewed obedience.

faq.q: Did Peter's denial end his usefulness?
faq.a: No. Jesus restored him and entrusted him with responsibility.

faq.q: What does restoration involve?
faq.a: It involves facing failure honestly, receiving Christ's grace and returning to faithful service.

lessons.t: Peter Filled with the Holy Spirit
lessons.hint: Contrast Peter's earlier fear with Spirit-empowered boldness, showing the Spirit's role in witness.
obj: Connect courage with dependence on God.
app: Teach that Spirit-filled ministry remains grounded in Scripture and centred on Christ.

faq.q: What changed Peter?
faq.a: The risen Christ had restored him, and Acts records the empowering presence of the Holy Spirit.

faq.q: What was central to Peter's Pentecost message?
faq.a: He proclaimed Jesus' death, resurrection, lordship and the call to repent and believe.

lessons.hint: Draw leadership lessons from Peter's life while keeping Christ as the model and Shepherd of the Church.
app: Create a culture where teachers can be corrected without defensiveness.
Leaders should model what they teach.

faq.q: Was Peter always right as a leader?
faq.a: No. Galatians 2 shows that Peter could act inconsistently and needed correction.

faq.q: What should Christian leadership look like?
faq.a: It should be willing service, humility, integrity and example under Christ's authority.

reserve.title: The Efficacy of Mercy
reserve.emph: Explore the power of God's mercy in forgiveness, restoration and Christian relationships.

lessons.hint: Ground the subject of mercy in God's revealed character and His compassion toward His people.
app: Teach mercy as God's character, not merely a human emotion.
Guard against comparing ourselves with others.

faq.q: Why does mercy matter to salvation?
faq.a: Believers depend entirely on God's gracious and merciful provision rather than their own righteousness.

faq.q: How should receiving mercy change us?
faq.a: It should produce humility, gratitude and mercy toward others.

lessons.hint: Show how God's mercy restores relationship while still taking repentance, truth and responsibility seriously.
obj: Learn how mercy and repentance interact.
app: Distinguish forgiveness from pretending harm did not happen.
Encourage wise restoration and accountability where appropriate.

faq.q: Does restoration mean trust is instantly restored?
faq.a: Not necessarily. Forgiveness and restoration of relationship can involve time, truth and rebuilding trust.

faq.q: Why was the older brother also challenged?
faq.a: The parable exposes self-righteousness and the failure to rejoice over restoration.

lessons.hint: Teach believers to resist harsh, partial and condemning attitudes while still respecting biblical justice and truth.
out: Mercy and the law of love.
app: Do not use 'do not judge' to forbid discernment.
Teach humility, truth and mercy together.

faq.q: Does mercy mean we cannot identify wrongdoing?
faq.a: No. Scripture calls believers to discernment while warning against hypocritical and self-righteous judgment.

faq.q: How does mercy triumph over judgment?
faq.a: It reflects God's compassionate character and refuses to treat others merely according to condemnation.

lessons.hint: Move the learner from receiving mercy to embodying mercy in family, church, workplace and community.
app: Identify one relationship where mercy is needed.
Respond to offence with prayer, truth and grace.
Serve people who cannot repay you.

faq.q: How can I show mercy without becoming a doormat?
faq.a: Mercy does not require abandoning wisdom or boundaries; it means responding with compassion rather than revenge.

faq.q: What is one practical way to become an instrument of mercy?
faq.a: Listen before judging, forgive where appropriate, help those in need and speak truth with love.

teachers.intro: Nine modules, basic to advanced, for every person who facilitates or teaches in this ministry. A teacher works through them in order. Module 1 includes the seven ways of handling the Word, which every teacher must know before standing anywhere.

modules.t: The Role of a Bible Teacher
modules.purpose: Settle who a Bible teacher is before dealing with how to teach: his character, his accountability and the seven different things he may be asked to do.
must: State plainly what a Bible teacher is and is not.
Name the seven ways of handling the Word and say which is called for in a given setting.
Accept correction from Scripture without taking it as a personal attack.
out: The teacher as servant of the Word, not owner of it.
Character and example: the teacher's life is part of the lesson.
Accountability: teachers shall receive the greater judgment.
The seven ways of handling the Word, and choosing the right one.
Remaining a learner: every teacher is first a disciple.
errors: Teaching in order to be seen as learned.
Refusing questions or correction.
Taking the title before the preparation.
modules.practice: Each teacher writes, in one page, what he believes a Bible teacher in this ministry is responsible for, and reads it to the group for comment.

ccc.q: Ignorance of the Scriptures is ignorance of Christ.

modules.purpose: Fix the aim of all our teaching: that the hearer sees Christ, and not the teacher, the programme or a moral lesson detached from him.
must: State the Christ-centred aim of any passage he teaches.
Show a passage's connection to Christ without forcing it.
Resist turning Bible characters into mere examples of success.
out: The one subject of the Scriptures.
On the road to Emmaus: the Lord's own method.
What it means to let the hearer go home with Christ, not only with advice.
errors: Reducing a passage to a motivational lesson.
Making the teacher's experience the centre.
Allegorising every detail until the text says anything you wish.
modules.practice: Take one Old Testament narrative. Prepare two short openings: one that treats it only as a moral example, and one that shows where it stands in God's plan in Christ. Present both; discuss the difference.

pope.q: All divine Scripture is one book, and this one book is Christ, speaks of Christ and finds its fulfilment in Christ

modules.purpose: Give the teacher the basic discipline of reading a passage where it actually stands, before saying what it means.
must: Identify author, audience, occasion and the flow of the argument.
Read the verses before and after before using a verse.
Say what kind of writing a passage is: narrative, law, poetry, prophecy, letter, gospel.
out: The passage in its paragraph; the paragraph in its book.
Who is being addressed, and under which covenant.
Literary forms and why they change how we read.
Historical and cultural background: enough, and not too much.
The unity of the whole of Scripture.
errors: Building doctrine on half a verse.
Treating a promise to Israel as an unqualified promise to us without asking how it comes to us in Christ.
Reading poetry as though it were law.
modules.practice: Give the group a well-known verse commonly quoted alone. Each person reads the whole chapter and reports what the context adds or corrects.

ccc.q: to the content and unity of the whole Scripture
ccc.note: the first of the Church's three criteria for interpreting Scripture

modules.t: Rightly Dividing the Word of Truth
modules.purpose: Teach sound interpretation: how a teacher reaches a conclusion from the text and can show his working.
must: Let the clear passages interpret the difficult ones.
Compare Scripture with Scripture and explain the connection, not merely stack references.
Say honestly where Scripture is less than clear, instead of inventing certainty.
out: The plain sense first; figures of speech recognised as such.
Reading within the living Tradition of the Church, and the coherence of the faith.
errors: Choosing the meaning that suits the point already decided on.
Quoting a chain of references that are not actually about the same thing.
Claiming certainty beyond what the text supports.
modules.practice: Each teacher takes one difficult passage and presents how he reached his conclusion, step by step. The group questions the steps, not the person.

ccc.q: the coherence of the truths of faith among themselves and within the whole plan of Revelation

modules.t: The Person and Work of Christ in Teaching
modules.purpose: Ground teachers in Christology, so that what they say about Jesus is accurate and not merely devotional.
must: State who Christ is: true God and true man, one Person.
Explain the saving work of the Cross and Resurrection without reducing it to an example of love.
Show how a doctrinal truth about Christ reaches practical life.
out: The Resurrection and the Lordship of Christ.
Christ the Head of his Body, the Church.
Teaching doctrine so that people can live on it.
errors: Speaking of Jesus only as teacher, example or healer.
Separating his divinity from his humanity in careless language.
Making the Cross an emotional story with no accomplishment attached.
modules.practice: In pairs, explain in three minutes to a hypothetical enquirer who Jesus is and what he has done, using no more than four Scriptures. Then shorten it to one minute.

ccc.q: God speaks only one single Word
ccc.note: his Son, in whom he expresses himself completely

modules.t: Law, Grace and Covenant for Teachers
modules.purpose: Give teachers a clear grasp of the two covenants, so that they neither preach law as though Christ had not come, nor grace as though holiness did not matter.
must: Explain the purpose of the law and its relation to the promise.
Teach justification as God's free gift without making obedience optional.
Recognise and correct both legalism and presumption in a group.
out: What the law was given to do, and what it could not do.
Justification: the free gift received by faith.
Grace that teaches us to live soberly and righteously.
Why fear-based teaching produces neither holiness nor peace.
errors: Loading believers with rules the Gospel does not impose.
Using grace as permission, which Scripture itself rejects.
Pitting St Paul against St James instead of reading both.
modules.practice: Prepare a ten-minute teaching on Ephesians 2:8–10, showing both that salvation is not of works and that we are created in Christ Jesus unto good works. The group tests whether both halves were honoured.

ccc.q: Grace is favor, the free and undeserved help that God gives us to respond to his call to become children of God
ccc.note: see also 2010: no one can merit the initial grace of forgiveness and justification

modules.purpose: Turn preparation into a lesson people can follow, and give the facilitator control of time and discussion.
must: State the central truth of the lesson in one sentence.
Build objectives, outline and application that serve that one truth.
Hold a discussion to the text and to the clock.
out: Writing objectives that can actually be met.
The shape of a session: opening, main text, supporting Scripture, application, questions.
Asking questions that open the text rather than test the group.
Managing the dominant speaker, the silent member and the question that derails.
errors: Preparing material instead of preparing a lesson.
Five points that are really five separate lessons.
Letting one person's story consume the session.
modules.practice: Each teacher prepares one lesson plan on a single page, presents the first ten minutes, and receives feedback on clarity, not delivery.

modules.t: Avoiding Doctrinal Error and Private Interpretation
modules.purpose: Protect the flock. Teach facilitators to recognise error, including their own, and to correct it without quarrelling.
must: Name the common errors that circulate in our environment and answer them from Scripture.
Distinguish a private opinion from the faith of the Church.
Correct error in a way that keeps the person.
out: Private interpretation and why Scripture warns about it.
The common errors we meet: fear teaching, curses and bloodline doctrines, prosperity as proof of favour, deliverance as a substitute for discipleship, visions taught as doctrine.
Marks of error: a verse removed from context, a new revelation, a teacher who cannot be questioned, fear used as leverage.
Teaching the whole counsel of God rather than a favourite theme.
How to correct: in love, from the text, in private where possible.
errors: Correcting in public to win.
Letting error pass to keep peace.
Treating every difference of opinion as heresy.
modules.practice: The group is given five statements commonly heard in church. Each teacher judges: sound, unsound, or a matter on which believers may differ — and must show from Scripture how he decided.

ccc.q: Read the Scripture within "the living Tradition of the whole Church"

modules.t: Teaching for Transformation, Not Just Information
modules.purpose: Carry the lesson from the head into the life, which is the only reason the lesson was given.
must: Close every lesson with what the hearer should believe, change, practise, avoid or become.
Teach in a way that engages conscience and will, not memory alone.
Follow up: ask next week what happened.
out: Knowledge that puffs up, and love that builds up.
From text to conviction to practice.
Application that is specific enough to obey.
The teacher's own life as the first field of application.
errors: Ending the lesson at the explanation.
Applications so general that nobody can act on them.
Demanding of the group what the teacher has not attempted.
modules.practice: Take a lesson already taught and rewrite its application into three specific, doable actions. Return next session and report what you yourself did.

workshop.intro: Eight sessions for advanced growth and depth, held as workshops and special sessions through the year. They are longer than the weekly study and more demanding: context, word studies, comparison of passages, doctrinal positions, teaching practice and extended questions. Teachers within the fellowship normally teach them; a sound guest teacher may be invited when the subject calls for it.

sessions.t: Christ in the Old and New Testament
sessions.purpose: See the two Testaments as one revelation, and learn to handle types, prophecy and fulfilment soundly.
out: One plan of redemption from Genesis to Revelation.
Promise and fulfilment: how the New Testament reads the Old.
Types rightly used: the Passover lamb, the bronze serpent, Melchizedek.
The limits of typology: respecting the original historical meaning.
Reading the Psalms and the Prophets with Christ in view.
discuss: Where does a type end and imagination begin?
How do we teach the Old Testament to people who have only been given moral stories?

pope.q: All divine Scripture is one book, and this one book is Christ, speaks of Christ and finds its fulfilment in Christ

sessions.t: The New Covenant Reality in Christ
sessions.purpose: Establish what is new in the new covenant, and what it changes for the believer now.
out: The promise of a new covenant in Jeremiah and Ezekiel.
The blood of the covenant and the one sacrifice.
The law written on the heart.
Access to the Father and the torn veil.
Living as a people of the new covenant.
discuss: What continues from the old covenant and what is fulfilled and finished?
How does the new covenant shape the way we come to the Eucharist?

ccc.q: Our justification comes from the grace of God.

sessions.t: Righteousness by Faith and Not by Works
sessions.purpose: Teach justification clearly, and hold together St Paul and St James without weakening either.
out: The righteousness of God revealed from faith to faith.
Justification as God's free gift, not a wage.
Abraham: the pattern of faith counted for righteousness.
St James and the faith that shows itself in works.
Why a believer can be certain and still be striving.
discuss: If justification is free, why does Scripture urge us to work out our salvation?
How do we teach this to people who have been taught to earn God's love?

ccc.q: no one can merit the initial grace of forgiveness and justification
ccc.note: see also 2011: the saints have always had a lively awareness that their merits were pure grace

sessions.t: Deep Study of the Epistles: the Pauline Revelation of Christ
sessions.purpose: Train teachers to read a letter as a letter, follow its argument, and draw doctrine from it responsibly.
out: Reading a letter whole: occasion, audience, argument.
Romans: the Gospel set out in order.
Ephesians and Colossians: Christ and his Body.
The Pastoral letters: sound doctrine and the care of a congregation.
Working through a paragraph: method demonstrated.
discuss: What do we lose by reading the Epistles only in single verses?
Take one chapter of Ephesians: trace the argument from first to last verse.

sessions.purpose: Teach the believer's standing — seated with Christ — and distinguish position from experience without losing either.
out: In Christ: the phrase that governs the Epistles.
Raised and seated with him in the heavenly places.
Security and sober watchfulness held together.
discuss: How do we teach a settled standing to people who feel far from God?
Where does this teaching go wrong when it is handled carelessly?

ccc.q: Grace is a participation in the life of God.

sessions.t: The Ministry of the Holy Spirit in the New Covenant
sessions.purpose: Set the Spirit's work in the believer and the Church on a doctrinal footing, which matters especially in a charismatic community.
out: The Spirit promised and poured out.
The Spirit in Baptism and Confirmation, and in the life of prayer.
Gifts, fruit and order in the assembly.
Discernment: testing what is claimed as the Spirit's work.
Why the Spirit always leads to Christ and to the Church.
discuss: How do we welcome the Spirit's gifts and still keep order and discernment?
What do we say to someone who believes a manifestation settles a doctrinal question?

ccc.q: it is Christ who is seen, the visible image of the invisible God, but it is the Spirit who reveals him

sessions.t: Sound Doctrine and Doctrinal Balance in Teaching
sessions.purpose: Equip teachers to hold the whole counsel of God, to weigh what is central against what is secondary, and to teach without riding a single theme.
out: What sound doctrine means and why it is called sound.
The whole counsel of God: teaching what we would rather skip.
Where believers may legitimately differ, and where they may not.
Balance: grace and holiness, faith and obedience, mercy and truth.
discuss: Name a doctrine we rarely teach here. Why do we avoid it?
How do we disagree with another teacher publicly without damaging the ministry?

ccc.q: the coherence of the truths of faith among themselves and within the whole plan of Revelation

sessions.t: Maturity: from Milk to Strong Meat
sessions.purpose: Press the community toward maturity, and give teachers a way to move a group from basic teaching to solid food.
out: Milk and strong meat in Hebrews and 1 Corinthians.
The marks of spiritual infancy and of maturity.
Senses exercised to discern good and evil.
Planning a group's progress over a year rather than a session.
discuss: Is our weekly study feeding milk to people ready for meat?
What would we need to change to move this community one stage forward this year?

defs.intro: Our people use these seven words as if they all mean the same thing, and that is where much confusion begins. A teacher is asked to exhort and preaches instead. A preacher is invited to teach and shares a testimony. Someone quotes a verse and calls it teaching. Before a teacher stands anywhere, he should know exactly which of these he has been asked to do, and be able to do that one well.

items.one: A guided, unhurried study of a passage with a group, where the text itself leads and everybody takes part.
items.what: Bible study takes a passage and works through it in context: who wrote it, to whom, what is being said, how Scripture elsewhere explains it, and what it means for us. It is not a speech. There are questions, answers, objections and discussion, and the facilitator keeps the group inside the text.
items.aim: Understanding. People should leave able to explain the passage themselves.
marks: The text is open in front of everyone.
Questions are welcomed, including difficult ones.
The facilitator asks more than he declares.
Nobody leaves with a conclusion the text does not support.
items.watch: The commonest failure is a facilitator who turns the study into a sermon and takes all forty minutes himself.

items.one: The careful, ordered explanation of doctrine and of the Scriptures, so that hearers understand and can build on it.
items.what: Teaching is instruction. It builds truth upon truth in an order the hearer can follow, defines terms, handles context, answers objections and leaves a structure in the mind. It is the gift Scripture names for the equipping of the saints, and it is accountable: a teacher can be asked how he reached his conclusion.
items.aim: That believers know the truth, are established in it and cannot be tossed about by every wind of doctrine.
marks: There is a clear central truth and an order to the material.
Scripture is explained, not merely quoted.
The teacher shows his working from the text.
The hearer could repeat the lesson to someone else.
items.watch: Teaching is the one most often confused with preaching. If your hearers felt a great deal and understood nothing new, you preached; you did not teach.

items.one: The proclamation of the message of Christ with authority, calling for a response.
items.what: Preaching announces. It is the herald's work: Christ crucified, risen and reigning, proclaimed so that hearers repent, believe, return or obey. It can be short, it is usually urgent, and it aims at the will. In our tradition the homily within the liturgy is preaching: it breaks open the word that has just been read and applies it to the life of the people.
items.aim: A response — conversion, repentance, faith, obedience, hope.
marks: Christ is announced, not merely discussed.
There is a call: believe, repent, forgive, rise, go.
It is addressed to the will, not only to the understanding.
items.watch: Volume is not authority. A quiet preacher who proclaims Christ has more authority than a loud one who proclaims himself.

items.one: A word of encouragement, comfort or urging that stirs believers to act on what they already know.
items.what: Exhortation (paraklesis) comes alongside. It does not usually bring new information; it strengthens, comforts, warns and urges people to keep going in what they have already been taught. It is pastoral and it is often brief. Barnabas, the son of encouragement, is its picture.
items.aim: Strengthening. The hearer leaves able to continue.
marks: It assumes the teaching and applies it.
It is warm, direct and short.
It encourages or warns; it rarely explains at length.
items.watch: Exhortation is not scolding. A word that leaves people flattened has not exhorted them.

items.one: Believers opening Scripture together and saying what it says and what it means for them, without one person teaching.
items.what: Sharing is mutual. A passage is read in a group and each person speaks: what the text says, what it stirs, how it touches their life. It builds fellowship and makes the word personal. It is what most of our small gatherings are actually doing.
items.aim: Personal engagement with the word and fellowship in it.
marks: Everyone speaks; no one dominates.
People speak about the passage, not around it.
A leader gently keeps it on the text.
items.watch: Sharing can drift into opinions and private meanings. Someone must hold the group to the text, or sharing becomes the place where error is first spoken aloud and nobody corrects it.

items.one: Speaking the Scripture itself — quoting, confessing, praying it back to God.
items.what: This is the simple act of putting God's own words on our lips: in prayer, in confession, in memorisation, in the liturgy, in resisting temptation as the Lord himself did. It carries no explanation and no application, and it does not need any. It is the word, said.
items.aim: That God's word is in our mouths and in our hearts.
marks: The words are Scripture's, not ours.
It is used in prayer, memory and spiritual warfare.
It is accurate: the verse is said as it stands.
items.watch: Saying a verse is not the same as teaching it. A quoted verse with no context has taught nobody, and a verse said as a formula to force God's hand is not faith but superstition.

items.one: Bringing the Gospel of Jesus Christ to those who do not yet know him, so that they may believe.
items.what: Evangelisation is the first announcement, directed outward. It is not catechesis and not Bible study: it is the news of what God has done in Christ, told to someone who has not received it, with an invitation to come to him. Everything else in this ministry assumes it has happened.
items.aim: Faith in Jesus Christ, and a life joined to him in his Church.
marks: It is directed to those who do not know Christ.
Its content is Christ's person and saving work, not our programmes.
It invites, it does not merely inform.
The messenger's life does not contradict the message.
items.watch: Do not assume everyone in the pew has been evangelised. Many have been catechised without ever having been told the Gospel personally.

pope.q: evangelization is first and foremost about preaching the Gospel to those who do not know Jesus Christ

defs.close: A mature teaching ministry can do all seven and knows which one is called for. When you are invited to minister, ask the question plainly: do you want a teaching, an exhortation, a sharing, or a homily? Then do that one, and do it well.

ccc.q: Ignorance of the Scriptures is ignorance of Christ.

qa.intro: The questions our teachers actually meet in the hall: from members, from enquirers, and sometimes from other teachers. Each is answered doctrinally and from Scripture, with the Catechism or a papal text added where it says the same thing. Use them to prepare, and read them before you teach the topic they belong to.

items.q: Is Christ really in the whole Bible, or are we reading him into the Old Testament?
items.a: He is genuinely there, because the whole of Scripture unfolds one plan of redemption that reaches its fulfilment in him. The Lord himself read it that way on the road to Emmaus.
p: The question is a fair one, because typology can be abused. The answer is that the connection is made by Scripture itself, not invented by us. Jesus, beginning at Moses and all the prophets, expounded unto them in all the scriptures the things concerning himself. The New Testament writers then do the same thing repeatedly: Christ our passover is sacrificed for us; as Moses lifted up the serpent, so must the Son of man be lifted up.

So the rule is simple. Where Scripture itself makes the connection, teach it confidently. Where it does not, you may still show how a passage stands within the one plan of redemption, but say that plainly rather than claiming a fulfilment the text does not make.

What we reject is the opposite error, which is far more common in our churches: teaching the Old Testament as a collection of disconnected moral stories about successful men. The Bible is not a book of heroes. It is one book about one Saviour.

pope.q: All divine Scripture is one book, and this one book is Christ, speaks of Christ and finds its fulfilment in Christ

chain.t: Beginning at Moses and all the prophets, he expounded unto them in all the scriptures the things concerning himself.
chain.s: The method is the Lord's own, not a teacher's invention.

chain.t: Search the scriptures… they are they which testify of me.
chain.s: The Scriptures were already testifying of him before a single Gospel was written.

chain.t: Christ our passover is sacrificed for us.
chain.s: The New Testament itself reaches back and names the Passover lamb as Christ.

chain.t: As Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, even so must the Son of man be lifted up.
chain.s: Jesus himself takes a bronze serpent in Numbers and says: that was about me.

chain.t: The Lamb slain from the foundation of the world.
chain.s: The plan did not begin at Calvary. Calvary revealed a plan older than creation.

items.christ: So the Old Testament is not a long wait before the real story. It is the same story, told in shadow, by a God who was describing his Son before his Son was born. When you open Genesis you are not reading about men who failed; you are reading about a God who was already moving toward a cross. Teach it that way and your hearers will stop looking for heroes to imitate and start looking for the Saviour who was there all along.

items.q: Does every single verse point directly to Jesus?
items.a: No. A sound teacher respects what a passage meant where it stands, and then shows where it sits in the one story that leads to Christ.
p: Not every verse mentions or foreshadows Christ. A genealogy, a building measurement or a proverb about a lazy man is doing its own work. Forcing Christ into every detail does not honour him; it teaches people a method of reading that can later be used to make Scripture say anything at all.

The Church's own rule for interpretation is to be attentive to the content and unity of the whole of Scripture, which has Christ at its centre. That is a different thing from squeezing a private meaning out of every line.
Teach the passage. Then show its place in the whole. That is both honest and Christ-centred.

ccc.q: to the content and unity of the whole Scripture

chain.t: All scripture is given by inspiration of God, and is profitable for doctrine, for reproof, for correction, for instruction.
chain.s: Every verse is profitable. That is not the same as every verse being a prophecy of Christ.

chain.t: All things must be fulfilled, which were written in the law of Moses, and in the prophets, and in the psalms, concerning me.
chain.s: The Lord points to the whole, not to every separate line.

chain.t: Of whom speaketh the prophet this?… Philip began at the same scripture, and preached unto him Jesus.
chain.s: Philip starts where the text is and moves to Christ. He does not force a meaning into it.

chain.t: No prophecy of the scripture is of any private interpretation.
chain.s: A meaning squeezed out of a detail, which nobody else can see in it, is private interpretation.

items.christ: The honest reading honours Christ more than the forced one. If you must twist a verse to find him, you are not showing people Christ; you are showing them your cleverness, and teaching them a method that will later be used to prove anything. Read the passage as it stands, then show where it sits in the one plan that ends in him. He is the centre of the whole; he does not need to be hidden in every corner.

items.q: Are we 'people of the book', like other religions that have a holy book?
items.a: No. We are people of a living Person. The Scriptures are God's inspired word, and they lead us to Christ, who is himself the Word.
p: This distinction matters for a teaching ministry, because it decides what a Bible study is for. We do not study to master a text. We study to meet the One the text reveals, and to be changed by him.

That is why the Church says Christianity is the religion of the Word of God, and the word is not a written and mute word but the Word incarnate and living. The Spirit must open our minds, or the letter stays a letter.
Practically: never end a study at information. Ask the group what they now see of Christ, and what they will do about it.

ccc.q: Christianity is the religion of the "Word" of God
ccc.note: not a religion of the book

chain.t: In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God.
chain.s: Before there was a written word there was a living Word, and he is a Person.

chain.t: And the Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us.
chain.s: The Word did not stay on a page. He took flesh.

chain.t: Ye will not come to me, that ye might have life.
chain.s: Men can master the text and still refuse the Person. That is the warning.

chain.t: The word of God is quick, and powerful, and sharper than any twoedged sword.
chain.s: The word is living because the One it reveals is living.

chain.t: Did not our heart burn within us… while he opened to us the scriptures?
chain.s: When the Scriptures are rightly opened, the result is a burning heart, not merely a full notebook.

items.christ: This is why a Bible study in this ministry must never end at information. The Pharisees knew the text and crucified its subject. Our aim is that a member leaves the hall seeing Christ more clearly than when he came, and loving him more. Ask it out loud at the end of every session: what did we see of the Lord today, and what will we do about it?

items.q: People say Catholics do not read the Bible. What do I answer?
items.a: Answer with the facts and then with repentance where it is deserved. The Church gives us Scripture at every Mass and urges all the faithful to read it frequently; where our people do not know it, the remedy is to teach them, which is exactly what this ministry exists to do.
p: The accusation is partly unfair and partly earned. Unfair, because the liturgy is saturated with Scripture: a Catholic who attends Mass hears the Old Testament, the Psalms, the Epistles and the Gospel every Sunday, and the Church urges the faithful to learn the surpassing knowledge of Jesus Christ by frequent reading of the divine Scriptures.
Earned, because many of our people have never opened the Bible at home and cannot find a book in it. We should not argue about that; we should fix it. That is the whole reason this committee exists.

So do not be defensive. Say what the Church teaches, admit the gap honestly, and invite the person to the study. A member who can open his Bible and explain a passage answers the accusation better than any argument.

ccc.q: Ignorance of the Scriptures is ignorance of Christ.

pope.q: how important it is for the People of God to be properly taught and trained to approach the sacred Scriptures

chain.t: Let the word of Christ dwell in you richly in all wisdom.
chain.s: Dwell richly is a settled, abundant indwelling, not an occasional visit.

chain.t: They received the word with all readiness of mind, and searched the scriptures daily.
chain.s: The Bereans are commended for checking an apostle against the text.

chain.t: From a child thou hast known the holy scriptures, which are able to make thee wise unto salvation through faith which is in Christ Jesus.
chain.s: Scripture's own stated purpose: wisdom unto salvation through faith in Christ.

chain.t: Thy word is a lamp unto my feet, and a light unto my path.
chain.s: A lamp is for walking, which means daily use, not display.

items.christ: Do not fight this one. Win it by producing people. A member who can open his Bible, find the passage, explain it in context and show you Christ in it has ended the argument without saying a word about it. That is the whole point of this ministry: not to defend our people, but to feed them, until the charge simply stops being true in our parish.

items.q: If Jesus said 'It is finished', what is left for us to do?
items.a: Nothing is left to add to the sacrifice; everything is left to receive and to live. The work of redemption is complete; our part is faith, which then works through love.
p: 'It is finished' is a declaration of completion, not of retirement. Christ accomplished the work the Father gave him, and Scripture says that after he had offered one sacrifice for sins for ever, he sat down. No further sacrifice is needed or possible.

What remains is not a contribution to the price but a response to the gift: believing, being baptised into his death and resurrection, living from his life, and growing in holiness. The Church's teaching holds both ends firmly: our justification comes from the grace of God, and we are then created in Christ Jesus unto good works.
Watch the two errors. One says the work is unfinished, and loads people with fear. The other says that because the work is finished, how we live no longer matters. Scripture refuses both.

ccc.q: Our justification comes from the grace of God.

chain.t: It is finished.
chain.s: One word in the original, used on receipts: the debt is paid in full.

chain.t: But this man, after he had offered one sacrifice for sins for ever, sat down on the right hand of God.
chain.s: The priests stood daily; he sat down. A seated priest means completed work.

chain.t: By one offering he hath perfected for ever them that are sanctified.
chain.s: Perfected, for ever, by one offering. Not a process we top up.

chain.t: By grace are ye saved through faith… not of works, lest any man should boast.
chain.s: Nothing of ours is added to the purchase.

chain.t: For we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus unto good works.
chain.s: The same sentence that excludes works as payment commands them as fruit.

chain.t: Work out your own salvation… for it is God which worketh in you.
chain.s: We work out what God has worked in. We do not work for it.

items.christ: Hold Ephesians 2:8-10 as one sentence, because Paul wrote it as one. Verse 9 kills pride; verse 10 kills laziness. What is finished is the work of redemption — Christ did it, and nothing can be added to it. What is not finished is you and me being conformed to his image. So the believer rests in what Christ accomplished and labours in what Christ is forming. Rest first, then work; never work in order to rest.

items.q: If the sacrifice was once for all, why do we speak of the sacrifice of the Mass?
items.a: Because the Mass does not repeat Calvary; it makes present the one sacrifice offered once for all, so that the Church may be joined to it and receive its fruit.
p: This is the question our members are most often asked by other Christians, and it is answered badly when teachers improvise. Hebrews is emphatic that Christ was offered once and that his sacrifice is not repeated. The Church teaches exactly that, and holds at the same time that in the Eucharist the one sacrifice of the Cross is made present to us.

The Lord said, do this in remembrance of me, and St Paul says that as often as we eat this bread and drink this cup we show the Lord's death till he come. It is one sacrifice, not many; and we are not spectators of it but participants.

Teach it with those words: not another sacrifice, and not merely a memory of a distant event, but the one sacrifice made present. Say what the Church says, and do not improvise explanations you cannot support.

chain.t: So Christ was once offered to bear the sins of many.
chain.s: Once. Scripture will not let us speak of repeated sacrifices.

chain.t: One sacrifice for sins for ever.
chain.s: The same emphasis again, deliberately.

chain.t: This do in remembrance of me.
chain.s: The Lord's own command, given the night before the one sacrifice.

chain.t: As often as ye eat this bread, and drink this cup, ye do shew the Lord's death till he come.
chain.s: We proclaim his death. The one death, shown forth.

chain.t: The cup of blessing which we bless, is it not the communion of the blood of Christ?
chain.s: Communion means a real sharing. We are not spectators of a distant event.

items.christ: Say what Scripture says and stop there: one sacrifice, never repeated, and a people really joined to it. The Cross is not re-done; we are brought in. Teach it with Hebrews open, so that your hearers see that the Church's own language rests on the very verses they are being quoted against. And let the point land where it should — at the Lord himself, offered once, and sufficient for ever.

items.q: The members say they do not feel like new creations. What do I tell them?
items.a: That their standing before God does not rest on feeling. What God has done in Christ is a fact to be believed, and the feelings follow the renewing of the mind, slowly.
p: Teach the order plainly: fact, faith, feeling. Scripture says if any man be in Christ, he is a new creature. That is stated as an accomplished fact, not as an experience to be achieved. Our feelings follow our thinking, and our thinking is renewed as the word is heard over time.

Be honest with them too. The new creation is in the spirit; the mind still carries what the village, the school and years of fear-teaching put there, and the body is not yet glorified. That is why Scripture commands the renewing of the mind rather than assuming it.
And give them something to do: a short passage about who they are in Christ, read and prayed daily for a month. The word does the work.

ccc.q: Grace is a participation in the life of God.

chain.t: If any man be in Christ, he is a new creature.
chain.s: Stated as a finished fact. Not a feeling to achieve.

chain.t: For ye are dead, and your life is hid with Christ in God.
chain.s: Your life is hidden. Hidden things are not seen, which is why feelings cannot find them.

chain.t: Be ye transformed by the renewing of your mind.
chain.s: The spirit was made new at once; the mind is renewed over time.

chain.t: Put off… be renewed in the spirit of your mind… put on the new man.
chain.s: Put off and put on are daily verbs. The new man is already there to put on.

chain.t: For we walk by faith, not by sight.
chain.s: Faith takes God's word over the evidence of the senses.

items.christ: Tell them the order and keep repeating it: fact, faith, feeling. The fact is Christ's finished work. Faith lays hold of it. Feelings follow eventually, and sometimes slowly. A believer who waits for the feeling before he believes the fact will wait for ever; a believer who believes the fact will find the feelings catching up. And give them something to do with their mouth and their eyes: a short passage about who they are in Christ, read daily for a month. The word does the renewing; we only keep showing up.

items.q: Does teaching 'identity in Christ' not make people proud?
items.a: It does the opposite when it is taught properly, because everything we are in Christ was given to us and none of it was earned.
p: Pride comes from thinking we achieved our standing. The New Testament teaching on identity removes exactly that ground: by grace are ye saved through faith, and that not of yourselves, it is the gift of God, not of works, lest any man should boast.

What this teaching does remove is false humility, which is really unbelief dressed up piously: the believer who keeps calling himself what God no longer calls him. Confidence in Christ and humility about ourselves grow together.
Where it goes wrong is when identity is detached from the Cross and becomes a message about human greatness. Keep it tied to Christ's work and it will humble people.

ccc.q: the saints have always had a lively awareness that their merits were pure grace.

chain.t: What hast thou that thou didst not receive?
chain.s: One question that ends every boast.

chain.t: Not of yourselves… not of works, lest any man should boast.
chain.s: Boasting is excluded by the manner of our salvation.

chain.t: God forbid that I should glory, save in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ.
chain.s: Paul keeps one boast and it is a cross.

chain.t: Ye are a chosen generation, a royal priesthood, an holy nation, a peculiar people.
chain.s: The highest language in Scripture about believers — and every word of it is a gift.

chain.t: Where is boasting then? It is excluded.
chain.s: Scripture closes the matter plainly.

items.christ: True identity teaching humbles, because every item on the list was bought by someone else. The proud man says look what I am. The believer says look what he has made me. And the false humility that keeps calling yourself what God no longer calls you is not modesty at all; it is disagreeing with him. Confidence in Christ and lowliness in yourself grow on the same stem, and that stem is the Cross.

items.q: A member cannot forgive herself for something long confessed. What do I say?
items.a: Tell her the truth: God has forgiven and forgotten it, and refusing to accept that is not humility, it is doubting his word. Then point her to the help the Church gives, and if the torment persists, to someone who can walk with her.
p: Scripture is blunt about God's side of this: their sins and iniquities will I remember no more; as far as the east is from the west, so far hath he removed our transgressions from us. If God has dealt with it, continuing to carry it adds nothing and changes nothing.

Make a distinction in her hearing between guilt, which the blood of Christ has answered, and consequences or memories, which may remain and need healing. Shame often outlives forgiveness, and it is relieved by the truth, not by more penance.

The sacrament of Penance exists precisely so that a Catholic may hear forgiveness spoken aloud rather than hope for it privately. Encourage her to receive it, and to stop confessing the same forgiven sin. If the torment does not lift, this may be more than a spiritual question, and there is no shame in speaking to someone who can help.

chain.t: Their sins and iniquities will I remember no more.
chain.s: God's own stated position on the matter.

chain.t: As far as the east is from the west, so far hath he removed our transgressions from us.
chain.s: A distance that cannot be measured, because east and west never meet.

chain.t: Thou wilt cast all their sins into the depths of the sea.
chain.s: Cast away, not filed for later.

chain.t: I, even I, am he that blotteth out thy transgressions for mine own sake.
chain.s: For his own sake. The motive is his, so our worthiness is not in question.

chain.t: There is therefore now no condemnation to them which are in Christ Jesus.
chain.s: Now. Not after enough sorrow has been produced.

chain.t: If our heart condemn us, God is greater than our heart.
chain.s: Scripture anticipates a heart that will not agree with God, and overrules it.

items.christ: Teach her the difference between guilt and shame. Guilt was answered at the Cross and is gone. Shame is a memory and a feeling, and it is healed by hearing the truth again and again. Her conscience says remember; God says I remember no more. Somebody has to be wrong, and it is not God. Point her to the sacrament, where forgiveness is spoken aloud to her, and then ask her to stop confessing a sin God has forgotten. If the torment does not lift, that may be more than a spiritual matter, and there is no shame in talking to someone who can help carry it.

items.q: St Paul says faith without works, St James says faith with works. Which is it?
items.a: Both, and they are not in conflict. Paul is denying that works earn justification; James is denying that a faith which produces nothing is real faith.
p: Look at what each is arguing against. Paul faces people who want to add law-keeping to Christ in order to be accepted: by the deeds of the law shall no flesh be justified. James faces people who say they believe and do nothing about it: what doth it profit, my brethren, though a man say he hath faith, and have not works?

They even use Abraham together: Paul says Abraham believed God and it was counted unto him for righteousness, and James says that faith was shown to be genuine when he obeyed years later. One speaks of how righteousness is received; the other of how it is recognised.
